transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A new study has found that drinking tea regularly is associated with a lower risk of heart disease and stroke, according to researchers at the University of Cambridge. The study followed over 100,000 adults for more than a decade and found that those who drank at least three cups of tea per day had a 20 percent lower risk of developing heart disease and a 24 percent lower risk of stroke compared to non-tea drinkers. Researchers say that tea contains flavonoids and other antioxidant compounds that help reduce inflammation and improve blood vessel function. Both black tea and green tea showed similar benefits. The study's authors say that drinking tea can be part of a heart-healthy lifestyle, along with a balanced diet and regular exercise.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: The city of Portland, Oregon has become the first major US city to ban single-use plastic straws, utensils, and stirrers in all restaurants, cafes, and food service businesses. The ban, which went into effect this year, requires food businesses to only provide these items upon customer request, and encourages the use of compostable or reusable alternatives. The city estimates that the ban will reduce plastic waste by over 100 million items per year. Portland has been a leader in environmental policies, previously banning plastic shopping bags in 2012 and charging a fee for paper bags. City officials say the new ban is an important step toward reducing plastic pollution and protecting marine ecosystems, as plastic waste often ends up in rivers and oceans where it harms wildlife.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley have developed a new type of solar panel that can generate electricity from rain as well as sunlight, making it possible to produce power even on cloudy, rainy days. The panels use a special coating that captures energy from the impact of raindrops, converting the kinetic energy of falling rain into electricity. While the energy generated from rain is less than what's generated from sunlight, it could provide a significant boost in rainy climates where traditional solar panels are less effective. Researchers say that this technology could make solar power more viable in regions with lots of rainfall, and could help increase the overall efficiency of solar energy systems. The technology is still in the experimental stage, but researchers are working to improve its efficiency and bring it to market.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Jake): Hey Zoe, I need your help. I've decided I need to learn how to cook.
Woman (Zoe): Really? That's great! What brought this on?
Man: Well, I went to the doctor last week for a checkup, and she said my cholesterol is too high. She told me I need to eat healthier and stop eating so much fast food and takeout.
Woman: Oh, that makes sense. Yeah, cooking at home is a great way to eat healthier. You can control what goes into your food.
Man: Exactly. But the problem is, I don't know how to cook anything. Like, I can barely make toast without burning it.
Woman: Ha, don't worry, everyone has to start somewhere. I'd be happy to teach you some basics.
Man: Really? That would be amazing! I was hoping you'd say that.
Woman: Of course! What kind of food do you like?
Man: I like pretty much everything. But I want to learn how to make simple, healthy meals. Things that are easy to make after work.
Woman: Okay, that's a good place to start. Let's think... we could start with something simple like pasta with vegetables, or a stir-fry, or maybe roasted chicken with vegetables.
Man: Roasted chicken sounds good. But isn't that hard?

Woman: Not at all! It's actually really easy. You just season the chicken, put it in the oven, and let it cook. While it's cooking, you can roast some vegetables at the same time. It's mostly hands-off.
Man: That sounds manageable. What do I need?

Woman: Well, you'll need some basic equipment—a good knife, a cutting board, a baking sheet, maybe a roasting pan. And of course, the ingredients: a chicken, some vegetables like potatoes, carrots, and broccoli, olive oil, salt, pepper, and some herbs or spices.
Man: Okay, I can get those. When can we do this?
Woman: How about this Saturday? I can come over in the afternoon and we can cook together. I'll bring some recipes and we can make a few things.
Man: Saturday sounds perfect! I'll make sure I have everything we need.
Woman: Great. And don't worry—cooking is really just about practice. The more you do it, the better you'll get. And once you learn a few basic techniques, you can make all kinds of different meals.
Man: I hope so. I'm actually kind of excited about this. It'll be nice to eat something I made myself.
Woman: It is rewarding! And your cholesterol will thank you too. Okay, I'll see you Saturday.
Man: See you Saturday, and thanks again Zoe. I really appreciate this.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Ava): Hey Ethan, I need your advice. I've been selling my handmade jewelry on Etsy for a few months now, and I'm not making as many sales as I'd hoped. Do you have any ideas?
Man (Ethan): Oh, that's frustrating. Let me think. First of all, what kind of jewelry are you making?
Woman: I make mostly necklaces and earrings with beads and wire. I try to make unique, one-of-a-kind pieces.
Man: That sounds nice. How much are you charging for your pieces?
Woman: Well, the necklaces are usually around $30 to $50, and the earrings are $15 to $25. I try to price them based on materials and time.
Man: Hmm, that seems reasonable. But have you looked at what other sellers are charging for similar items? You want to be competitive, but you also don't want to underprice yourself.
Woman: Yeah, I've looked at other shops. Some are cheaper, some are more expensive. It's hard to know where to price things.
Man: I understand. What about your photos? Are they good quality? On Etsy, photos are really important because people can't see the items in person.
Woman: I take photos with my phone. They're okay, but maybe not great. I don't have a good camera or lighting setup.

Man: That could be part of the problem. Good photos make a huge difference. You don't need an expensive camera—you can take great photos with your phone if you have good lighting. Try taking photos near a window in natural light, and use a plain background.
Woman: That's a good tip. I'll try that. What else?
Man: What about marketing? Are you using social media to promote your shop?
Woman: I have an Instagram account, but I don't post very often. Maybe once a week or so.
Man: You should post more often—at least a few times a week. And you could try TikTok too, showing the process of making your jewelry. People love seeing how things are made.
Woman: TikTok? I don't know... I'm not very good at making videos.
Man: It doesn't have to be fancy! Just short clips of you working on a piece, or showing a finished product. Authenticity is more important than production quality.
Woman: Okay, I'll think about it. What about the Etsy platform itself? Are there things I can do to get more visibility on Etsy?

Man: Yeah, definitely. Make sure your titles and descriptions use good keywords that people would search for. And use all 10 tags that Etsy allows—those help with search. Also, Etsy has promotional tools you can use, like running sales or offering free shipping.
Woman: Free shipping? But that would eat into my profits.

Man: I know, but studies show that free shipping encourages people to buy. You could build the shipping cost into the price of the item instead. And you could offer free shipping on orders over a certain amount to encourage people to buy more.
Woman: That's a good idea. I could try that.
Man: And don't forget about reviews! Ask your customers to leave reviews after they receive their items. Good reviews help build trust and make new customers more likely to buy.
Woman: Yeah, I have a few reviews, but not many. I'll start asking for them.
Man: You're already doing great by having the courage to start your own business. It takes time to build up a customer base. Be patient and keep trying new things.
Woman: Thanks, Ethan. This has been really helpful. I feel more motivated now.
Man: No problem! Let me know how it goes. I'd love to see your shop succeed.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Female)
paras: The history of writing is one of the most important developments in human civilization. Before writing was invented, information could only be passed down orally, which meant it could be lost or changed over time. Writing allowed humans to record information, preserve knowledge, and communicate across distances and generations.

The earliest known writing systems developed independently in several different parts of the world. The oldest known writing system is cuneiform, which was developed by the Sumerians in Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) around 3500 BCE. Cuneiform was written by pressing a wedge-shaped stylus into soft clay tablets, which were then baked to harden them. It was used for thousands of years throughout the Middle East for everything from record-keeping to literature.

Around the same time, the ancient Egyptians developed hieroglyphics, a system of picture symbols that represented objects, ideas, and sounds. Hieroglyphics were often carved into stone monuments and painted on the walls of tombs and temples. The Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799, was key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphics, as it contained the same text in hieroglyphics, Demotic (a simpler Egyptian script), and ancient Greek.

In China, writing developed independently around 1200 BCE during the Shang Dynasty. The earliest Chinese writing was found on oracle bones—turtle shells and animal bones that were used for divination. Chinese writing is logographic, meaning each character represents a word or concept, rather than a sound like in alphabetic systems. Chinese characters have evolved over thousands of years but are still in use today.

The Maya civilization in Central America also developed a complex writing system independently, around 300 BCE. Maya writing combined logograms and syllabic symbols, and was carved into stone monuments, painted on pottery, and written in folding books called codices.

The alphabet, where each symbol represents a single sound, was a later development. The first alphabet was developed by the Phoenicians around 1000 BCE, and it became the basis for many modern alphabets, including Greek, Latin, and eventually English.
Writing has evolved enormously over the millennia, from clay tablets to digital text, but its fundamental purpose—recording and sharing information—remains the same.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Male)
paras: The placebo effect is a fascinating phenomenon in medicine where a person experiences real health improvements from a treatment that has no actual medical effect—like a sugar pill or a saline injection. The word "placebo" comes from Latin and means "I shall please." The placebo effect demonstrates the powerful connection between the mind and the body, and it has important implications for medicine and healthcare.

The placebo effect was first systematically studied in the mid-20th century, when researchers began using placebo-controlled trials to test new medications. In these trials, one group of patients receives the actual medication, while another group receives a placebo. Neither the patients nor the doctors know who is getting which treatment. Researchers found that in many cases, patients who received the placebo also showed improvement, sometimes as much as 30 to 40 percent of patients.

How does the placebo effect work? There are several theories. One is that when people expect to get better, their bodies actually produce chemicals like endorphins and dopamine that can reduce pain and improve mood. Another theory is that the ritual of receiving treatment—going to a doctor, taking a pill, being cared for—triggers a healing response in the body. The patient-doctor relationship and the confidence in the treatment also play a role.

The placebo effect isn't just in people's heads—it can produce real, measurable physiological changes. Studies have shown that placebos can affect heart rate, blood pressure, brain activity, and even immune system function. In one famous study, patients with Parkinson's disease who received a placebo showed actual changes in brain activity and improvement in motor symptoms.

There's also a phenomenon called the "nocebo effect," which is the opposite of the placebo effect. When people expect a treatment to have negative side effects, they may actually experience those side effects, even if the treatment is inert. This shows that expectations can work in both positive and negative directions.

The placebo effect raises important ethical questions in medicine. While it can be beneficial, doctors generally shouldn't prescribe placebos without telling patients, as that would be deceptive. But understanding the placebo effect can help doctors better support their patients' healing process by fostering positive expectations and a strong doctor-patient relationship.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Urbanization—the process by which people move from rural areas to cities, and cities grow in size and population—is one of the most important trends of the modern era. In 1800, only about 3 percent of the world's population lived in cities. Today, more than 55 percent of people live in urban areas, and that number is expected to rise to 68 percent by 2050. Understanding urbanization is essential for planning for the future and building sustainable, livable cities.

Urbanization has been driven by many factors. Industrialization was a major driver, as factories created jobs in cities and drew people from rural areas. Economic opportunities—better jobs, higher wages, more diverse employment—continue to draw people to cities. Cities also offer better access to education, healthcare, cultural institutions, and social services. And in many developing countries, rural poverty, conflict, and environmental factors like drought and desertification push people to move to cities.

Urbanization has many benefits. Cities are centers of innovation, creativity, and economic growth. They bring people together, fostering the exchange of ideas and the creation of new businesses and technologies. Dense urban areas can also be more efficient in terms of energy use, transportation, and resource consumption per person than sprawling rural or suburban areas. Public transportation, shared infrastructure, and higher population density can reduce per capita environmental impact.

But urbanization also presents significant challenges. Rapid, unplanned urbanization can lead to overcrowding, inadequate housing, and the growth of informal settlements or slums, where people lack access to clean water, sanitation, and basic services. Traffic congestion, air pollution, noise pollution, and waste management are common problems in growing cities. And as cities expand, they often encroach on agricultural land and natural habitats, leading to loss of biodiversity and increased environmental pressure.

The challenges of urbanization are particularly acute in developing countries, where cities are growing fastest and often lack the resources and infrastructure to keep up with population growth. But even in developed countries, cities face issues like housing affordability, inequality, and aging infrastructure.

Addressing these challenges requires thoughtful urban planning and policy. Building sustainable cities means investing in public transportation, creating green spaces, ensuring access to affordable housing, improving waste management, and reducing pollution. It means designing cities that are livable, equitable, and resilient.

The concept of the "smart city"—using technology and data to improve city services and quality of life—is one approach that many cities are exploring. But technology alone isn't enough; good governance, community engagement, and equitable development are also essential.
